title: Who is my neighbor? (Luke 10:25–37)
hook: a lawyer's question and a story that asks who acted like a neighbor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus rejoicing that things hidden from the wise were revealed to babes. Your line was revealed to babes. Who did you listen to that you might have overlooked? Day five hundred forty-one.

It starts as a test. A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, stands up and asks: "Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns it back: what does the law say? How do you read it? And the lawyer answers well, joining two lines from his own scriptures, from Deuteronomy and Leviticus: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus says: right. "This do, and thou shalt live." But the lawyer, Luke says, wanting to justify himself, asks one more question. A question about where the edges are.

"And who is my neighbour?" Who counts? Where can I stop? Jesus answers with a story. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead." It's a steep, lonely road through the desert hills. A priest comes along and passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, does the same. The text doesn't tell us why. People have guessed for centuries, fear, hurry, worry about touching what might be a corpse, but Luke is silent. Then a Samaritan comes. Samaritans and Jews had generations of bad blood between them, and the people listening would not expect a Samaritan to be the hero. "And when he saw him, he had compassion on him." The same word Luke used for Jesus at Nain, moved in the gut. He bandages the wounds, pouring in oil and wine. He puts the man on his own animal and walks. He pays an innkeeper two coins, roughly two days' wages, and says: "Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee." Then Jesus flips the lawyer's question. Not who is my neighbor, but this: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Notice that the lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; many readers think he couldn't bring himself to. He says: "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus: "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted a boundary. He gets a verb. Neighbor isn't a category of people you owe. It's something you become.
screen: `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR? WHERE DO I STOP?`
`A PRIEST, A LEVITE: THE OTHER SIDE.`
`NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO WAS A NEIGHBOR.`
then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a neighbor to someone unexpected. Settle, and breathe. Think about your own road: the commute, the street, the hallway at work, the group chat. Who's lying by the side of it? Not literally, maybe. Someone who's been left out, knocked down by bad news, stuck. And now the harder part: think of someone you wouldn't expect to help, or wouldn't expect to help you. Someone from the other side of some line, politics, faith, class, a family feud. Hold them in mind without arguing. Picture crossing the road toward them, the way the Samaritan did. What would one small act of mercy look like? If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply picture the crossing. The bell holds the time.
Who is my neighbor? A lawyer's question, and Jesus' story of a Samaritan who stops on the road, so the question becomes: who acted as a neighbor?
Your line: go and do likewise. Cross one road today toward someone you'd usually pass by, and do one small, practical thing. Day five hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: The Good Samaritan is one of the best-known stories in Christian teaching, and many hospitals, charities and laws that protect people who help in emergencies carry the Samaritan's name.

fork.setup: you're a Samaritan on the Jericho road. a man from the other side of an old feud lies beaten and half dead. what do you do?

bandage him, put him on your animal, and pay for the inn.

original.note: Greek: near, nearby, the one near you. the word behind "neighbor."

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to strangers.
what it means: the lawyer asks who counts as his neighbor, and Jesus turns it into who acted as one. neighbor becomes a verb.
what a scholar hears: "neighbor" is plesion, the one near. Jesus' question moves it from who is near me to whom I draw near to.

notes: The priest and Levite: the script says the text is silent on their reasons and lists common guesses without endorsing one, so as not to make temple workers or Jewish law the foil. Keeper to confirm.
'Two coins, roughly two days' wages' assumes a denarius as a day's wage (Matthew 20:2). Confirm.

Reviewer edit: 'The lawyer can't quite bring himself to say the word Samaritan' was stated as fact; now 'the lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; many readers think he couldn't bring himself to.' Confirm.
Samaritan-Jewish hostility described as mutual and historical.
'Laws that protect people who help' refers to Good Samaritan laws in many places. General.
